title: Blessed are you poor (Luke 6:20–26)
hookLine: Luke's beatitudes are blunt, with woes to the rich

lines: A NIGHT OF PRAYER, THEN DOWN.
A PLAIN PLACE, A GREAT CROWD.
cards: Matthew sets the beatitudes on a mountain: blessed are the poor in spirit. Luke tells a different scene. Jesus has spent the night praying on a mountain, picked his twelve, and come down.
He stands, Luke says, in a plain place, a level stretch of ground, with a great crowd from Judea, Jerusalem and the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon. Sick people push to touch him.
He lifts his eyes to his disciples and speaks, and what he says is shorter than Matthew's version, and sharper.

teach.b: Luke's first beatitude, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God." Not poor in spirit. Poor.
And not they. You. Jesus is looking at real people in front of him and talking straight to them.
Luke has four blessings: you poor, you who hunger now, you who weep now, you who are hated for his sake. Then he turns the coin over with four woes.
The first: "But woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation." Woe to you that are filled, for you shall hunger. Woe to you that now laugh.
Woe when all men speak well of you. Each blessing has its matching woe.

teach.h: WOE AS A CRY: ALAS FOR YOU.
teach.b: Some readers hear woe not as a curse but as a cry of grief: alas for you. On that reading, Jesus isn't wishing harm on the comfortable; he's warning that comfort can be the whole reward, and then it's spent.
So which is it, poor or poor in spirit? Catholics read both Gospels as true and hold them together. Matthew names the heart that knows it needs God.
Luke won't let that become only an inner feeling: real hunger and real poverty are what God sees first.

teach.h: A PREFERENTIAL LOVE FOR THE POOR.
teach.b: The Catechism speaks of the Church's preferential love for the poor, and says that love is inspired by the Gospel of the beatitudes.
Some saints took Luke literally. Francis of Assisi handed even his clothes back to his father, in front of the bishop, and walked away with nothing.

how: Catholics hear Luke's sermon on the plain at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and parishes run food pantries, Saint Vincent de Paul conferences and collections for the poor as a regular part of parish life.

games.q: what does “blessed are you poor” mean?
o: Luke's first beatitude, spoken to the poor face to face
a saying that poverty itself makes a person holy
Matthew's blessing on those who are poor in spirit

games.q: the sermon on the plain — tap the pairs.
p: blessed are the poor in spirit
woe to you that are rich
read as a cry of grief: alas

s: Luke's sermon is set on a mountain, like Matthew's
Luke says Jesus came down and stood in a plain place.
Luke pairs each blessing with a matching woe
four blessings, four woes: poor and rich, hungry and filled, weeping and laughing, hated and praised.
Catholics have to choose between Matthew's and Luke's beatitudes
the Church reads both as true and holds them together.

games.q: you're hearing this on the plain, and you're comfortable: fed, warm, well liked. Jesus says woe to you that are rich. what is he doing?
o: warning you that comfort can be your whole reward.
games.why: woe can be read as a cry of grief, alas for you. the comfortable have their consolation already, and it can run out.

practice: Think of who you're likely to pass today: someone outside a store, a coworker who's struggling, a family on a parish list.
Pick one, decide what you could give, money, food, time, a real conversation, and picture looking them in the eye, the way Jesus looked at the crowd on the plain, as people he called blessed.
If you pray, hold that person before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Blessed are you poor. Luke's first beatitude, spoken face to face on a level plain, paired with a woe for the rich. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the poor, the word used for beggars. Luke's word for the people Jesus calls blessed.

carryVoice: Your line: blessed are you poor. Not they, but you, face to face. That's day four hundred fifty-three.

sources.q: Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
